name: Moral Luck
description: Once outcomes are known, people often morally re-grade the same action by what happened afterward, even when that outcome was partly outside the actor's control. Bad luck can make identical judgment look more blameworthy than good luck.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to incident postmortems, trust-and-safety sanctions, marketplace disputes, autonomous-system failures, appeals flows, and internal blame culture. Teams can punish or praise by result rather than by what the actor could reasonably control.
myth_risk_note: Empirical backing exists for outcome-sensitive blame specifically as tracking false beliefs rather than mere bad outcomes (Young, Nichols & Saxe 2010), but the philosophical concept of moral luck is much broader (encompassing resultant, circumstantial, and constitutive forms). Labeling this one narrow empirical finding with the full philosophical umbrella term risks overstating its scope.
prevalence_note: Recognizable in moral philosophy, legal theory, and some responsible-AI or algorithmic-accountability discussions, but the exact label remains uncommon in everyday product-design practice; teams more often describe the mechanism as judging by outcomes.

findings.description: Participants' moral-luck beliefs predicted harsher judgments of offenders based not only on intent but also on whether harm actually occurred. Prompting people to consider alternative outcomes, especially worse ones, reduced these luck-sensitive blame judgments.
findings.source_title: Beliefs in moral luck: When and why blame hinges on luck

findings.description: When evaluating past decisions, people rated the very same decision process as better when it led to a good outcome and worse when it led to a bad outcome, even though outcome quality was not a clean indicator of how sound the original decision process was. Baron and Hershey named this distortion 'outcome bias.'
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
